catalog_quote: This contact had the effect of shifting the main stress of the prosodic word from the penultimate syllable to the final syllable, which then became heavy and could include a moraic final consonant. [p.159] ... As contact intensified, there was a wholesale shift to a word-final stress pattern in Chamic [p.164] ... Rade and Jarai are closely related members of one of the two Highlands Chamic subgroups. While both have undergone additional reduction towards monosyllables, Rade has in general progressed much further than Jarai. Rade generally preserved initial consonants including h, but allowed several new cluster types at the cost of deletion of the first vowel. Like Western Cham, unstressed vowel neutralization has occurred in both Rade and Jarai, with later developments occurring in Rade conditioned by the preceding consonant if one existed. [p.177] ... (81) Pre-Rade əka:n - Rade ka:n '…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Rade (rade1240) is not in the catalog. The only title-matched bibliography item, Scales, Aubergé & Aycard 2023 (Interaction Studies 24: 131-168, doi 10.1075/is.22010.sca), is a human-robot-interaction paper on robot 'movement prosody'; Glottolog's own record labels its Rade code a 'computerized assignment from \"hri\"', so it is irrelevant (priority none). Re-reading the sources already (Norquest 2005 pp.159, 177; Thurgood & Li 2007 pp.129-130; Thurgood 1998 p.61; Đoàn 1993; Shintani 1981; Phan Văn Phức 1993; Y Tru Alio 2014) gives a consistent comparative picture — Chamic word-final (iambic) stress, Rade reduced furthest toward monosyllables with unstressed first-vowel neutralization/deletion — but no first-hand synchronic statement of a Rade word-stress rule. Best available statement is Norquest 2005 (comparative). Highest-value unread sources remain Thurgood 1999 (From Ancient Cham to Modern Dialects, OL Special Publ. 28; JSTOR/paywalled) and Đoàn Văn Phúc 1996 Ngữ âm tiếng Êđê (print only, cited by Y Tru Alio 2014 p.36). the rade1240 directory.

new_statements.rule_in_words: As in all mainland Chamic, the Rade prosodic word is right-headed: stress is on the final (main) syllable; the pretonic syllable is unstressed, its vowel neutralised to schwa or deleted, so that most Rade words have become monosyllables with initial clusters and any surviving presyllable is a stressless [Cə] (iambic/sesquisyllabic). Primary descriptions (Shintani 1981 p.121; Đoàn Văn Phúc 1993) accordingly analyse Rade as 'pratiquement monosyllabique' (C1)(C2)C3V(C4) with only an excrescent [ə] inside clusters, i.e. one full, prominence-bearing syllable per word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned for Rade in any source read (Norquest mentions secondary stress only for Proto-Malayo-Chamic trisyllables).
new_statements.exceptions: Norquest pp.178-179: a residue of Rade words keeps an unstressed initial syllable (vowel-initial ataw 'ghost', asaw 'dog'; kəŋa 'ear'); Shintani p.121-122 notes loss of initial /a-/, /ê-/ presyllables is frequent (asar ~ sar 'grain'). Y Tru Alio 2014 pp.38-40: function words mơng, kơ are weaker/faster in the sentence and any syllable can be emphasised for information focus (phrase level). Loans (zapone 'Japon') are polysyllabic (Shintani).
new_statements.domain_note: Norquest's/Thurgood's statements are diachronic-comparative (prosodic word of Proto-Chamic and its Rade reflexes, data via Thurgood 1999 < Tharp & Y-Bhăm 1980 etc.), not a fieldwork description of Rade citation forms. The synchronic primary sources read (Shintani 1981, informant from Buôn Ma Thuột; Đoàn Văn Phúc 1993, Kpă dialect) give no accent rule because they treat the word as a single syllable(me); Phan Văn Phức 1993 p.17 explicitly notes the absence of 'trọng âm từ' (word stress) as a cue in Ede compounds, and Y Tru Alio 2014 describes Ede as monosyllabic, non-tonal and syllable-timed with only utterance-level emphasis.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources refer to Rade/Êđê [rad] = rade1240. Đoàn Văn Phúc 1993 describes the Kpă dialect (xã Ea Tam, Buôn Ma Thuột); Shintani 1981's informant was a Buôn Ma Thuột speaker; Norquest 2005's Rade forms come from Thurgood 1999 (ultimately Tharp & Y-Bhăm 1980, Lee 1966, Egerod 1978). Nguyen 2013 describes Bih [ibh], a separate Highlands Chamic lect formerly counted as an Ede dialect — its iambic-stress statement should not be transferred to rade1240 without note.

new_statements.reading: Comparative-historical, not a synchronic description of Rade: Chamic main stress is word-final (iambic: unstressed presyllable + stressed final main syllable), and Rade has gone furthest toward monosyllables by neutralizing/deleting the unstressed first vowel (PC bula:n > Rade mlan 'moon'). Read together with Thurgood & Li 2007 pp.129-130 (Chamic 'stress switched to final position'; Rade msah 'wet' as the intermediate collapse stage) and Thurgood 1998 p.61 (PC iambic), the consistent picture is: Rade words are largely monosyllabic, and where a presyllable survives it is unstressed with prominence on the final (main) syllable, i.e. fixed final stress in the residual sesquisyllables. No source read gives a first-hand synchronic word-stress rule for Rade itself: Đoàn 1993 (thesis summary) replaces weak/strong-syllable notions with a single 'syllabeme', Shintani 1981 calls Rade practically monosyllabic with no accent statement, Phan Văn Phức 1993 says Ede compounds lack 'trọng âm từ', and Y Tru Alio 2014 (pp.36-40) describes only phrase-level emphasis and syllable-timed rhythm. this search of works with stress in the title's single title-matched item added nothing.
